## Overview

I built a multicycle processor that runs a subset of the 32-bit RISC-V base integer
instruction set (RV32I). The single-cycle processor from *Digital Design and Computer
Architecture: RISC-V Edition* uses separate instruction and data memories. This design uses
**one shared memory** and reuses **one ALU** for everything. Each instruction runs over 3–5
clock cycles, and a finite-state machine in the control unit sequences it.

Supported instructions: `lw`, `sw`, `add`, `sub`, `and`, `or`, `slt`, `addi`, `andi`, `ori`,
`slti`, `beq`, and `jal`.

My main contributions:

- **Datapath** (`datapath` in `top.sv`): the non-architectural registers (`OldPC`, `Instr`,
  `Data`, `A`, `WriteData`, `ALUOut`) that hold values between cycles, plus the `SrcA`, `SrcB`,
  `Result` and address multiplexers that route the shared ALU and memory.
- **Main FSM decoder** (`maindec.sv`): an 11-state Moore machine that sets every select and
  write-enable signal for each instruction type.
- **Verification**: a self-checking testbench runs the standard `riscvtest` program. It passes
  only when the value 71 is stored to address 84.

## Try it: interactive datapath

The simulator below is a cycle-accurate model of my RTL, ported signal-for-signal to
JavaScript. Step through the program one clock at a time. The highlighted wires show the
data moving through the datapath in the current FSM state. The tags on the multiplexers and
registers show the control signals the FSM is driving. Copper-colored blocks are written on
the next clock edge.

## How the simulator was verified against the RTL

I ran the SystemVerilog in Icarus Verilog with a tracing testbench. It prints the FSM state,
`PC`, `Instr`, `RegWrite`, `Result`, `MemWrite`, the memory address and `WriteData` on every
rising clock edge. The JavaScript model prints the same trace format, and I diffed the two over
400 cycles of both programs above. They match on every cycle of both programs. The only
differences are register and memory values that are still uninitialized `x` in the RTL (the
model treats them as 0), and cycles after the PC runs off the end of the 64-word memory.
:::

## The control FSM

| State | Name | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| S0 | Fetch | `Instr ← Mem[PC]`, `OldPC ← PC`, `PC ← PC + 4` (ALU computes PC+4) |
| S1 | Decode | Read `rs1`/`rs2` into `A`/`WriteData`; ALU precomputes `OldPC + imm` (branch/jump target) |
| S2 | MemAdr | `ALUOut ← A + imm` (load/store address) |
| S3 | MemRead | `Data ← Mem[ALUOut]` |
| S4 | MemWB | `rd ← Data` |
| S5 | MemWrite | `Mem[ALUOut] ← WriteData` |
| S6 | ExecuteR | `ALUOut ← A op WriteData` |
| S8 | ExecuteI | `ALUOut ← A op imm` |
| S7 | ALUWB | `rd ← ALUOut` |
| S9 | JAL | `PC ← target`, `ALUOut ← OldPC + 4` (then S7 writes `rd`) |
| S10 | BEQ | ALU subtracts; if `Zero`, `PC ← target` |

: Main decoder states. Loads take 5 cycles; R-type, I-type and `jal` take 4; stores and branches take 3. {.striped .hover}

## Synthesis results

I synthesized the RTL with the open-source [Yosys](https://github.com/YosysHQ/yosys) flow for a
Lattice iCE40, the same FPGA family as the UPduino used in E155. Then I placed and routed it with
nextpnr. The processor core (`RISCVmulticycle`) uses:

::: {.stat-grid}
::: {.stat}
[2,312]{.stat-num}
[4-input LUTs]{.stat-label}
:::
::: {.stat}
[1,220]{.stat-num}
[flip-flops]{.stat-label}
:::
::: {.stat}
[31]{.stat-num}
[carry cells (ALU adder)]{.stat-label}
:::
::: {.stat}
[~58 MHz]{.stat-num}
[F~max~ on iCE40 HX8K]{.stat-label}
:::
:::

| Module | LUT4 | Flip-flops | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `RegFile` | 1,833 | 992 | 31 × 32-bit registers (x0 hard-wired); two asynchronous read ports dominate the LUT count |
| `alu` | 143 | — | plus 31 `SB_CARRY` cells for the 32-bit add/subtract |
| `mux3` × 3 | 192 | — | `SrcA`, `SrcB`, `Result` |
| `mux2` | 32 | — | memory address select |
| Datapath registers | — | 224 | `PC`, `OldPC`, `Instr`, `Data`, `A`, `WriteData`, `ALUOut` |
| `maindec` | 32 | 4 | 11-state FSM (4-bit state register) |
| `Extend` | 15 | — | I/S/B/J immediate generation |
| `aludec` + `controller` | 6 | — | |

: Per-module breakdown from `synth_ice40 -noflatten`. The flattened total is slightly higher because Yosys optimizes differently across module boundaries. {.striped .hover}

About 80% of the logic is the **register file**. Its two asynchronous read ports become
32:1 multiplexers built from LUTs, because iCE40 block RAM only supports synchronous reads.
Changing the register file to synchronous reads would let it fit in block RAM and free most of
the LUTs. The control logic, by contrast, takes fewer than 40 LUTs.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Reproduce the synthesis

```bash
pip install yowasp-yosys yowasp-nextpnr-ice40
yowasp-yosys -p "read_verilog -sv top.sv maindec.sv; synth_ice40 -top RISCVmulticycle -json core.json; stat"
yowasp-nextpnr-ice40 --hx8k --package ct256 --json core.json --pcf-allow-unconstrained --freq 12
```

The timing run uses the larger HX8K because the core's 130 unconstrained I/O ports don't fit
the UP5K's 39-pin package.
:::
